Costly signaling theory in evolutionary psychology is the best explanation for why AI slop irks people (even in people who haven't picked a side in the AI race). Having the ability to create art in the real world displays signals of being able resource-saturated in other walks of life to the point that you have extra resources (like time and energy) to actually create art. 

AI art loses that signal.

Actually, this applies to a lot of art that can be cheaply faked (stencil copies, printouts, etc).

candidates.text:
Ben Horowitz on the rap group he started at 18, and why hip-hop became the source material for how he thinks about business:

"I was probably 12 when Rapper's Delight came out... The first one where I was really like, 'Oh, this is gonna be very different,' was when Run-DMC's Hard Times came out. This has a whole other feel to it than anything I've heard."

"The thing that made me locked into hip-hop: I went to school in New York. I have this friend who I grew up with who had gotten shot in the face in some kind of gun accident, and he was blind... I'd call home to my mom: 'Is he gonna be okay?' She's like, 'He hasn't spoken to anybody since he's been shot.'"

"Being a dumb 18-year-old kid, I was like, 'Hip-hop is so great. You can have nothing and you'll rap about your shoes. He needs that feeling.' So I would record the DJ Red Alert and Chuck Chill Out show. Everybody else would be out Saturday night, and I'd be recording. And I would send him the tapes."

"Then I called home to see how he's doing, and they're like, 'Well, he's talking now, but all he'll talk about is hip-hop.'"

"When I went out that summer, we started a hip-hop group called The Blind and Def Crew. Blind and D-E-F. We rapped about being blind. I wrote most of the lyrics: 'The Blind Def Crew, you know we're fly. Three of us, but we got four eyes.'"

"Hip-hop is very business oriented, particularly in the early days. When I started writing on business, so many of the ideas came from those old hip-hop songs. So I started putting the lyrics at the top of the post to give credit where credit was due."

@bhorowitz w/ @MotownIni

The endless battle to bridge translation from ambiguous grammars to unambiguous grammars in the search for precision continues.

For obvious reasons the last attempt at this - lowcode/nocode - was a fail.

So now we reach for less ambiguous specifications like ASD-STE100 implemented in english (rightly so).

But here's the rub - ambiguity exists first and foremost in the mind of the specifier, and llms create the illusion of productivity because they fill this gap with their own assumptions.

Most acquirers don't want to work on their acquired companies. They want to be investors.

They want the founders to continue running it for a small salary and a meager rollover equity. But founders want to work on their next big thing.

Most founders want to move on not just because the company hasn't hit escape velocity, but also because they have other big ideas and high opportunity cost.

Founders pick fast growth and new ideas over slow growth and low ownership. Always.

When founders talk to us at Helium Ventures, we always ask them to take the path of their biggest outcome.

Sometimes, it means taking care of customers, the team, investors, or themselves.

Pick the path of freedom and the biggest outcome.
